title: Thrill to the Stunning Bicameral Mind Hypothesis
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Julian Jaynes's 1976 bicameral mind hypothesis, which proposes that humans were not conscious in the modern sense until roughly 3,000 years ago; earlier people heard gods' commands as auditory hallucinations and obeyed them automatically. They cover how agriculture and larger societies created novel situations, how writing and metaphor-based language led to introspective consciousness, the Late Bronze Age collapse and the rise of oracles and religion, Jaynes's reading of the Iliad and the Ludlul bel nemeqi poem, split-brain research and the left-brain interpreter theory, theory of mind in children, and voice-hearing. The episode ends with a listener mail about press freedom and banned books in Sweden.
topics: The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind

entities.name: The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind

segments.title: Opening banter and sources
segments.summary: Hosts banter about approaching fifty and introduce the topic, based on a HowStuffWorks article by Robert Lamb, noting related sources such as Slate Star Codex and Less Wrong.

segments.title: Julian Jaynes and the bicameral mind defined
segments.summary: Jaynes, an outsider psychologist, proposed in the mid-1970s that consciousness emerged roughly one to two thousand years ago. Bicameral people heard gods' commands as auditory hallucinations and obeyed them without reflection, and the gods were culturally supported and felt real to them.

segments.title: Consciousness as a narrow definition
segments.summary: Discussion of whether bicameral people were literally zombies or automatons, and Jaynes's point that consciousness is a much smaller part of mental life, illustrated with the flashlight metaphor.

segments.title: Consciousness versus automatic behavior and the dishwasher example
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the difference between modern self-reflective thought and bicameral obedience, and the dishwasher analogy for routine versus novel situations, noting that simpler ancient life had fewer novel situations.

segments.title: Agriculture, large societies, and writing ending the bicameral mind
segments.summary: Jaynes linked the bicameral mind to agricultural society, larger populations and social control by rulers, and said the mind lasted roughly seven thousand years before writing made the commands fixed and readable, weakening it.

segments.title: Metaphor and language as the basis of consciousness
segments.summary: Hazard's Less Wrong post on recession metaphors illustrates how people think metaphorically; Jaynes argued that metaphor, enabled by sophisticated language, produced consciousness. Literal-minded characters in film, such as Randy Quaid in Kingpin, illustrate this, and children's literalism and theory of mind are discussed.

segments.title: Late Bronze Age collapse, loss of gods, and origins of religion
segments.summary: The Late Bronze Age collapse coincided with the timing Jaynes proposed; he argued people felt abandoned by silent gods, leading to nostalgia-driven religion, oracles, omens, and superstition. Jaynes also read the Iliad and a Mesopotamian poem literally as evidence of divine voices.

segments.title: Split-brain research, left-brain interpreter, and voice hearing
segments.summary: Split-brain surgery patients show one hemisphere acting without knowing why, and the left hemisphere confabulates explanations, supporting the left-brain interpreter theory. The hosts discuss the Julian Jaynes Society leader, voice hearing in the general population, children's imaginary friends, and the theory's ongoing scientific reception.

segments.title: Listener mail on press freedom and banned books
segments.summary: Alice Antonsen, a school librarian in Sweden, writes about teaching students about disinformation and displaying banned books, and plans to visit the Dowitt Isaac Library of censored books.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and invite listener email.
